conservative

/kuhn-SUR-vuh-tiv/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Something that is conservative is liking tradition and cautious of change.

His conservative approach to investing avoided any risky stocks.

Example

The head chef of a fifty-year-old restaurant is deeply conservative, guarding his grandmother's recipes word for word. When a young cook proposes trendy fusion dishes, he refuses: the menu will stay exactly as it has always been, because it has always worked.

He prefers the traditional way and is deliberately cautious about anything new, which is precisely the attitude conservative describes. Conservative is more precise than 'old-fashioned' because it names an intentional preference for tradition and caution, not simply being out of date.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

traditional: Traditional describes the customs and ways themselves -- long-established and handed down, like a traditional dance. Conservative describes an attitude toward those ways: preferring the tested path and staying cautious about change. A holiday song is traditional; the family that never lets the playlist change is conservative.

conventional: Conventional means conforming to widely accepted standards -- doing things the way most people currently do them. Conservative goes further: it actively favors tradition and resists change, rather than just fitting in. A conventional choice follows today's crowd; a conservative one holds to how things have long been done.

old-fashioned: Old-fashioned means behind the times -- out of date, whether or not anyone chose that. Conservative names a deliberate preference: liking tradition and staying cautious about change on purpose. An old-fashioned phone is simply outdated; a conservative buyer keeps using it because the familiar has always worked.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

radical: favoring extreme and sweeping change

innovative: eager to introduce brand-new methods

Where it sits · how strongly it resists change

careful → cautious → conservative → rigid

careful vs. conservative: Careful is weaker than conservative — a careful person avoids obvious risks, while a conservative person prefers the tested, traditional path in most things.

cautious vs. conservative: Cautious is slightly weaker than conservative; a cautious planner hesitates before changes, but a conservative one actively favors keeping things as they are.

rigid vs. conservative: Rigid is stronger than conservative — a conservative thinker is slow to change, while a rigid one refuses to change at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — con-: together; thoroughly (Latin)

root — serv: to keep, guard (Latin (servare))

suffix — -ative: tending to (Latin)

Put it together: Con- (thoroughly) + serv (keep, guard) + -ative (tending to): conservative describes someone tending to guard and keep things as they are — favoring tradition and caution over change.

Use the root in a new word: preserve: Volunteers met on Saturday to discuss how best to preserve the old theater downtown.

Root Check

Word Choice

Conservative fits a cautious, tradition-favoring political or social stance (a conservative voter, a conservative approach to reform) — keep it in that temperamental/political register rather than unrelated everyday uses like a 'conservative estimate.'
